TASK ID: sat-to-clique

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from SAT to Clique. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is SAT and TARGET is Clique. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = Sat
SAT (CNF satisfiability).

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[literal, ...], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * A clause is a list of any number of literals, including none.
    Literals may repeat, and a clause may contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes). An empty
clause [] can never be satisfied, so any formula containing one is no.

TARGET = Clique
Clique.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a clique of AT LEAST k vertices: k vertices with an
edge between every two of them.

Edge cases: k <= 0 is always yes. k = 1 is yes whenever n >= 1. k > n is
always no.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-4hh6s87u
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

Before submitting, check your reduction. Write tests in test_reduce.py that compare the brute-force solvers in problems.py on many small source instances and their reductions, run them, and revise reduce.py until the tests pass. Finally write verdict.json as {"verified": true or false, "tests_run": <int>, "tests_passed": <int>}, where verified is true only if all of your tests pass. Then submit.

{"command":"cd /tmp/reduction-4hh6s87u && cat > reduce.py <<'EOF'
"""Polynomial-time reduction from SAT to Clique.

Construction (the standard Karp reduction):

  * For every clause C and every literal occurrence l in C, create a vertex
    labelled (clause_index, literal).
  * Join two vertices with an edge iff they come from *different* clauses and
    their literals are not complementary (i.e. one is not the negation of the
    other).
  * Set k = number of clauses.

Correctness:
  (=>) A satisfying assignment makes at least one literal true in every clause.
       Pick one true literal per clause.  Chosen vertices lie in distinct
       clauses and no two are complementary (both are true under the same
       assignment), so they form a clique of size k.
  (<=) A clique of size k must use at most one vertex per clause (same-clause
       vertices are never adjacent) and there are exactly k clauses, hence it
       uses exactly one vertex per clause.  The chosen literals are pairwise
       non-complementary, so setting each chosen literal to true is consistent
       and satisfies every clause.

Edge cases:
  * No clauses -> k = 0, empty graph -> "at least 0" clique -> yes (SAT yes).
  * An empty clause contributes no vertices; then k = #clauses exceeds the
    number of vertices, so no clique of size k exists -> no (SAT no).
  * Repeated literals / repeated clauses simply create extra vertices; the
    same-clause non-adjacency keeps at most one chosen per clause, so nothing
    breaks.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    """Reduce a SAT instance to a Clique instance."""
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    # Vertex i corresponds to (clause_index, literal).
    vertices = []  # list of (clause_index, literal)
    for ci, clause in enumerate(clauses):
        for literal in clause:
            vertices.append((ci, literal))

    n = len(vertices)
    edges = []
    for i in range(n):
        ci, li = vertices[i]
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            cj, lj = vertices[j]
            if ci == cj:
                continue
            if li == -lj:
                continue
            edges.append([i, j])

    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": len(clauses)}
EOF
echo written"}
